item.title: [CBS News World] Iranian women are facing not just lashings, but "honor killings"
item.description:
Helia Fattahi told her parents she was pregnant. She was not married. They allegedly killed her.
Iranian police arrested both parents after the killing on Nov. 21 in Sanandaj, a city in the mountains of western Iran. According to local media, they confessed, citing the shame they believed their daughter had brought upon the family.
The provincial police chief, however, described the motive in more prosaic terms, calling it "family disputes," and the parents have not been charged with any crimes.
Two days later, in the holy city of Qom, another Iranian woman was violently punished for a different act of defiance.
Parastoo Ahmadi, a celebrated singer, and four members of her production team each received 74 lashes over a concert she had performed nearly two years earlier without wearing a headscarf.
Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi was lashed 74 times Monday by Iranian authorities for "outraging public decency" by singing without a hijab in a 2024 concert.
One woman had defied the conventions of her family. The other had defied the laws of the state.
Both cases, along with a spate of killings of young women across Iran in recent weeks, illuminate the sharp and still fragile limits to the modest freedoms Iranian women have secured since a popular uprising shook the Islamic Republic four years ago.
At the heart of that struggle are questions about who gets to decide how Iranian women live — what they wear, whom they love, and whether they can marry who they choose.
The protests first erupted in 2022 after Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman, died in police custody after being arrested for wearing her headscarf improperly. Her family told CBS News she was tortured in custody.
Women discarded their hair coverings, challenged the authority of Iran's morality police, and asserted freedoms that...

The death toll from the collapse of a six-story building under construction in southern Pakistan has risen to eightByThe Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 8:48 AM
KARACHI, Pakistan -- The death toll from the collapse of a six-story building under construction in southern Pakistan rose to eight Friday after rescuers recovered four more bodies, officials said.
Rescuers are still searching for about 10 people believed trapped beneath the rubble of the building, which collapsed Wednesday in Karachi’s Baloch Colony neighborhood, police official Raja Sarwar said.
Relatives of those still missing were in tears as they prayed for their safety.
On Friday, helmeted rescuers carried a body wrapped in a white covering on a stretcher across a mound of shattered concrete and tangled steel bars. Others were trying to reach into gaps in the wreckage in a congested residential area.

The 2026 Israeli elections were termed the most consequential in recent decades for the country – for multiple reasons.
For Benjamin Netanyahu, the caretaker prime minister, and his right-wing coalition, the elections were about keeping the far-right in power to protect the formative changes they enacted in state policies and institutions. For the anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot – or the “change bloc”, as it is referred to – the promise was to replace the failed October 7 government as they termed it, rehabilitate Israel’s international standing, and end internal divisions.
Once the results were announced, things changed. Gadi Eisenkot was tasked with forming Israel’s next government. But his bloc does not have enough seats in the Knesset to win a vote of confidence on its own. The United Arab List and the Joint List, parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, have 19 seats and are willing to back Eisenkot in his efforts to replace Netanyahu as Israel’s premier. But some in the change bloc, such as Avigdor Lieberman, promised not to support any government coalition that includes an Arab-led party or one that depended on votes from Palestinian citizens of Israel.

item.title: [ABC News World] A Ukraine loan is in limbo after EU budget talks stall. Leaders will try again in 3 weeks
item.description:
A Ukraine loan is in limbo after EU budget talks stall. Leaders will try again in 3 weeks
European Council President António Costa says European Union leaders have failed to agree on the 2028-2034 budgetByLORNE COOK Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 7:23 AM
BRUSSELS -- After struggling to chaperone Europe’s leaders through more than 12 hours of high-stakes budget negotiations, European Council President António Costa faced reporters early Friday with a stark assessment. “We didn’t reach an agreement,” he said.
Government leaders from the 27-nation European Union failed to narrow down the size of the 2028-2034 budget — let alone how it might be used. An important loan for Ukraine was caught up in the wrangling.
The spending package is small compared to national budgets — around 1% to 1.2% of gross national income — but it encapsulates the ambitions of the world’s biggest trading bloc and how it sees itself on the international stage.
Costa said “some member states asked for further reductions" in how much they would have to pay in, according to his latest proposals, while most were "opposed to further cuts, and some even proposed to reverse some cuts.”
It was a day of brinksmanship that saw the leaders playing tough for national audiences.
In three weeks, they will try again. The stakes are high. Elections in some key countries are approaching, and new hardline governments or shaky coalitions could complicate matters further.
In coming days, Costa will draw his conclusions from the summit talks — held in two plenary sessions, several group meetings, and the corridor conversations that typify EU budget negotiations — and consult again with capitals.
Some leaders, notably from countries that pay more into the budget than they get back in allocations, skipped certain meetings. But Costa, a former Portuguese prime minister, was unruffled.
“This is a negotiation process,” he said. “It’s normal that the member states try to defend their own national interests.” ...

item.description:
Zelenskyy urges the US to pressure Putin, calling Trump’s 'my friend' remark strange
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expressing frustration with the U.S. approach to Russian leader Vladimir PutinBySAMYA KULLAB Associated Press and ELISE MORTON Associated PressNovember 27, 2026, 6:22 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy expressed frustration with the U.S. stance toward Russian leader Vladimir Putin, in the latest sign of deepening tension between Kyiv and Washington just as a question mark appears over Europe’s future financial commitments to Kyiv.
Zelenskyy said in an interview with the BBC broadcast Friday that he wants the U.S. to apply more pressure on Putin to stop his invasion of Ukraine, which began almost five years ago and grinds on despite President Donald Trump’s efforts to broker a peace deal.
The Ukrainian president described Trump calling Putin “my friend” at a recent summit in China as “strange” because the Russian leader is “an aggressor and a killer.”
“He can’t be a friend,” Zelenskyy told the British broadcaster in Kyiv, likening it to Adolf Hitler being viewed as a friend in World War II.
The International Criminal Court has issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine. The Trump administration, meanwhile, has imposed sweeping sanctions on the court as part of its campaign to dismantle the tribunal over investigations into the U.S. and its allies including Israel.
Zelenskyy’s comments were broadcast a day after Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law and a U.S. envoy trying to mediate an end to the war, complimented Putin on being a “grandmaster” of politics and weeks after Kushner’s partner in peace efforts, Steve Witkoff, described Putin as a “humanitarian.”

Watch: Roofs torn off and streets under water as severe weather hits the USByJames FitzGeraldPublished4 hours ago
Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after severe weather hit both coasts of the United States during the Thanksgiving holiday.
Eastern areas were lashed on Thursday by a powerful storm which brought high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding. Pennsylvania remained the state worst hit by power cuts early on Friday, according to monitoring site Poweroutage.us.
Conditions are forecast now to improve, though the National Weather Service (NWS) cautions that it will take some time. The West Coast has also been affected by its own storms.
Flight disruption also persists, with hundreds more delays and cancellations reported on Friday - which is expected to be another busy travel day.
More than 2,500 flights within, into or out of the US were delayed on Thursday, and more than 450 were cancelled, according to Flightaware.com.
One passenger told the BBC he had been stuck at New York's LaGuardia Airport for 13 hours while trying to fly to see friends in Chicago for Thanksgiving.
Beyond the travel disruption, impacts were widespread across the East Coast, and US President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds.
Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds, while waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.
On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport.
The number of homes reporting power cuts peaked at close to a million on Thursday evening - with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey badly affected.

Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.
In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.
Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
He said talks were expected to resume in December.

item.title: [BBC World] Leaders clash in final Spain election debate as housing dominates run-in
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Jangling keys has turned into a symbol of protest against Spain's housing strugglesByNick BeakeEurope correspondent, Reporting fromValenciaPublished8 hours ago
Spain's main party leaders have made their last pitch to voters in a fractious final TV debate that focused heavily on the country's housing crisis.
Spaniards go to the ballot box on Sunday, with opinion polls suggesting Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez will fail to extend his eight years in office.
The debate on Thursday night marked the culmination of a campaign, which has been defined by the din of house keys being jangled in symbolic protest, rather than any carefully crafted words of politicians.
The struggle many face in opening the door to an affordable home has led to demonstrations filling plazas across the country.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo of the conservative People's Party (PP), who is poised to replace Sánchez, told viewers he would build a million new homes.
The PP, which is narrowly projected to be the largest party, is poised to form a government with the Vox party which is polling in third place.
If Vox do win a share of power at a national level, it would be the first time for the far right in Spain's 50 years of democracy since Francisco Franco's dictatorship.
Vox's leader Santiago Abascal told the debate only he cared about those who had the greatest housing need.
Ada Colau, who heads a left-wing coalition of four small left-wing parties called Broad Front, said taxing rich and exploitative landlords was urgently required.
Rejecting criticism that he had failed to tackle the country's housing problem, Sanchez talked up his recent emergency measures designed to protect tenants and cap rents.

Mr So's parents, both in their 80s, were among the 168 people killed in last year's Hong Kong tower-block blaze - the deadliest the city had seen in decades.
Their building was the first of the Wang Fuk Court complex to catch fire, and their bodies were burned beyond recognition.
In this video Mr So, who is only using his surname, visits his parents' grave and shows what is left of his parents' possessions.
Read more on this story.

On 26 November last year, Hong Kong saw its worst fire in decades.
The inferno that engulfed Wang Fuk Court burned for 43 hours, killing Christy's husband and 167 others. The previous day the couple had been celebrating their eldest daughter’s ninth birthday.
Christy, who only wants to use her first name, tells the BBC how she and her children are coping, one year on.
Read more here.

item.title: [BBC China] A renovation was meant to improve these Hong Kong homes - it ended in a blaze that killed 168
item.description:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.
This video can not be playedFigure caption,
Watch: Christy says she still sends WhatsApp messages to her husband who died in the blazeByGrace Tsoi, BBC World Service, Phoebe Kong, BBC Chinese , Reporting fromHong Kong and Yvette TanPublished25 November 2026
It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.
At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it.
It was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user - was trapped inside their home.
"I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC.
When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police.
She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said.
Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second - an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found.
It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, said the report.
"It was ferocious… I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau.
She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer.
